newsitem.title: USA: Ceridian frees chairman to spearhead growth.
newsitem.headline: Ceridian frees chairman to spearhead growth.

text.p: Ceridian Corp, which has taken steps to allow its chairman to focus on acquisitions and joint ventures, will also benefit from its decision to move a proven division manager into a challenging new role, analysts said on Wednesday.
Ceridian appointed Ronald Turner, head of its Computing Devices International (CDI) unit, to manage its day-to-day operations as a new member of its executive office.
"This is a positive thing," Gregory Gieber, an analyst at Smith Barney, said. "Turner is a very good manager who has done wonders at (Ceridian's) defense electrical business."

The Minneapolis-based information services and defense electronics company said making Turner a member of its upper management ranks would allow Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Lawrence Perlman to focus on strategic development and revenue growth.
Michael Geran, an analyst at Pershing/Division of Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette, agreed that the Turner appointment would free Perlman to explore strategic options.
"Turner is one of their better managers and his appointment lets Perlman do what he has said he wants to do, which is get his hands dirty again," Geran said.
But, Geran cautions, "the easy part is over if they want to continue growing at a rate of 15 percent or more."
"(Perlman) has to figure out how to take the company to the next level, considering the changes in the information services business," Geran said.

Turner, who joined Ceridian in 1993, has led a division whose revenue has grown about six percent a year and whose its gross margins has improved to seven and a half percent from six percent, according to Robert W. Baird & Co analyst Kimberly Stulo.
"Turner has done a fantastic job on building the CDI business," Stulo said.
"Perlman has said he wanted to get back to plotting strategic acquisitions and joint ventures. (Turner's appointment) does just that," she said.
Stulo said CDI accounted for about 37 percent of Ceridian's sales in 1996 and 21 percent of operating income.
Smith Barney's Gieber said the move would also allow Ceridian to keep a talented manager from becoming stale.
"This is about keeping good talent inside the company. (Turner) is a great manager but not in Ceridian's core business," Gieber said.
"The area Turner ran was clearly not part of Ceridian's future. The question for Ceridian becomes, how do you keep talent like that from leaving?" Gieber said.
Ceridian shares were up 2-1/2 at 37 early Wednesday afternoon.
